questions.q: Which fields of science does the chapter say the topics of the book are drawn from?
questions.a: Physics, chemistry, biology and earth sciences
o: Physics, chemistry, biology and earth sciences
Physics, chemistry, biology and mathematics
Physics, astronomy, geography and earth sciences
Chemistry, biology, earth sciences and technology

questions.q: (a) Name any two of the four fields of science that the chapter says the book's topics come from. (b) Why does the chapter say that these fields, though they appear as different chapters, should not be treated as separate boxes?
questions.a: (a) Any two of physics, chemistry, biology, earth sciences. (b) They are all interconnected: ideas in one area often inspire discoveries in another, or at least allow us to ask questions in another.
s: Part (a): names two of the four fields
Part (b): says they are interconnected and ideas in one inspire questions in another

questions.q: Which of these is NOT something the chapter says activities and experiments do for us?
questions.a: End the need for any further questions
o: End the need for any further questions
Serve as stepping stones to a deeper understanding of the environment
Help us see science as an ongoing process of discovery
Help us understand our place on this planet

questions.q: Imran folds a paper plane with a sharp nose and predicts it will fly farther than a blunt one. It does. He decides to try a heavier sheet next. Which idea in the chapter does his decision show?
questions.a: A result that fits our expectation can still raise questions needing more experiments
o: A result that fits our expectation can still raise questions needing more experiments
A result that fits our expectation ends the investigation for good
A result is worth noting only when it differs from the expectation
A second experiment is needed only when the first one fails

questions.q: Ravi says, 'Science is only about big, faraway things like the Sun and the stars, so a haldi stain or a sour fruit is not a science question.' Do you agree? Support your answer from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the world of science covers everything, small and large, near and far: tiny cells inside a leaf as well as the movement of the Sun and stars, and the materials we test at home. It begins its tour with sour fruits and a haldi stain, so Ravi's claim is wrong.
s: Verdict: Ravi is wrong
Evidence: science covers small and large, near and far, with a chapter example
Links to the chapter's own opening examples (sour fruits, haldi stain)

questions.q:
Match each line in Column I with what the chapter links it to in Column II.
Column I: 1. Early inventors studying bird wings  2. Topics from physics to earth sciences  3. Activities and experiments  4. Human activities and the natural world
Column II: a. Interconnected, so ideas in one inspire another  b. A dream of flying that began with simple observations  c. Stepping stones to a deeper understanding  d. A link that brings responsibility

Read the statements.
Statement 1: Ideas in one field of science never help us in another.
Statement 2: The chapter says science can help address environmental challenges.

questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q: (a) Name two of the three kinds of deeper questions the chapter says Grade 7 will ask. (b) Taking one of them, write a question of that kind about the pattern of rainfall in your town through the monsoon.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: How do things work? Why do events happen the way they do? What can we learn from the patterns we see in nature? (b) For example, 'What pattern is there in the days when rain falls, and why?' (a question of the pattern kind).

Part (b): writes a rainfall question that clearly belongs to one of the kinds

questions.q: Besides discovery, the chapter says science is also about
questions.a: responsibility, because human activities are linked to nature and society
o: responsibility, because human activities are linked to nature and society
freedom from the natural world and from society
control over the natural world through discovery alone
competition between scientists to be the first to discover

questions.q:
The drain beside a Class 7 classroom in Kochi overflowed into the school garden on some days of a 30-day rainy month. Three groups made plans. Group A: build a model of the drain and pour water through it. Group B: note the rainfall every day and mark the days the drain overflowed. Group C: look up the answer and copy it. After the month, Group B's record shows heavy rain on 15 days, and the drain overflowed on 12 of those days and on no other day.
(a) Which group(s) are following the chapter's advice to step out of the book? Give the chapter's reason for it.
(b) What share of the heavy-rain days had an overflow?
(c) Does Group B's record prove that heavy rain is the only cause of overflow? Explain.
(d) The school can fund only one group first. Choose between A and B and justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) A and B, because activities and experiments are stepping stones to a deeper understanding of the world; C only copies. (b) 12 of 15 = 80%. (c) No. On 3 heavy-rain days there was no overflow, so other things also matter, and the pattern raises further questions to test. (d) Either choice with reasoning; for example B first, because its record shows a pattern (80% of heavy-rain days) that can guide what the model in A should test.
s: Part (a): picks A and B with the stepping-stone reason
Part (c): says no, because 3 heavy-rain days had no overflow
Part (d): chooses A or B and justifies it using parts (b) and (c)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter treats physics, chemistry, biology and earth sciences as having no connection with one another.
Reason (R): In the book these topics appear as different chapters.
questions.a: Assertion is false but Reason is true
o: Assertion is false but Reason is true
Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false

questions.q: Why does the chapter ask us to step out of the book and out of the classroom at times? Give two points.
questions.a: To experience the world through activities and experiments, and because these are stepping stones to a deeper understanding of the environment we live in and of our place on this planet.
s: Says we experience the world through activities and experiments
Says they lead to deeper understanding of the environment and our place on the planet

questions.q: Hema's friend says, 'I now see that human activities are linked to what happens in nature.' Describe a situation from your school or town that could lead a student to say this, and write one question she could ask next.
questions.a: Any sensible situation: for example, plastic cups left in the school field after a function that choke the drain. The link is that our activity changes something in the natural surroundings. A next question: 'How many cups are left after each event, and what can reduce it?'
s: Describes a believable situation of a human activity
Shows the link to the natural world
Writes a follow-up question

questions.q: Kabir notices that ants in his school ground always walk in a single line to the canteen bin. He decides to note the time they appear each day for a week. According to the chapter, what is he doing?
questions.a: Asking what can be learnt from a pattern seen in nature
o: Asking what can be learnt from a pattern seen in nature
Collecting facts with no question behind them
Doing something that is not science because ants are not in the book
Studying only the Sun and stars, as science always does

questions.q: Mukesh says, 'If ideas in one field help another, the chapters can be read in any order.' Do you agree? Use two statements from the chapter.
questions.a: Not necessarily. The chapter says each chapter builds on what you already know, so order matters; it also says the fields are interconnected, which means ideas travel between chapters, not that the order is unimportant.
s: Gives the verdict that the claim does not follow
Uses the statement that each chapter builds on what you already know
Uses the statement that fields are interconnected, without dropping the order

questions.q: The Science Club of a school in Madurai plans a 'Science Week' with three activities. Choose three activities (describe each in a line) and for each say which idea from the chapter it serves, such as asking how or why, looking for patterns, stepping out of the book, or responsibility to the environment.
questions.a: Any three sensible activities, each matched to a different idea. For example: noting how the school pond level changes each day (patterns in nature); building and testing a paper plane (experiments as stepping stones); a collection drive for used batteries and a question about where they go (responsibility).
s: Activity 1 with its chapter idea
Activity 2 with its chapter idea
Activity 3 with its chapter idea
The three activities use three different ideas
Each activity is a real activity, not just reading

questions.q:
The Eco Club of a school in Mysuru counted plastic cups found in the field each week: Week 1, 40; Week 2, 35; Week 3, 90 (the week of Annual Day); Week 4, 45. Two proposals are placed before the Principal. Proposal X: no plastic cups at any event, with steel tumblers hired for each event. Proposal Y: a cleaning team collects cups after each event, with no change in what is served.
(a) Which week stands out, and which human activity is behind it?
(b) How many times as many cups were found in Week 3 as the average of the other three weeks?
(c) Which of the two things the chapter says human activities are linked to is most affected here?
(d) Choose X or Y and justify with the data and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Week 3, because of the Annual Day function. (b) Average of the other weeks = (40+35+45)/3 = 40; 90/40 = 2.25 times. (c) The natural surroundings (the field and drain), and through them the school community. (d) Either with reasons; for example X, because the jump is tied to events, so removing cups at the source tackles the pattern, while Y treats the effect only. A defence of Y for the weeks that are not events is also acceptable.
s: Part (a): Week 3, the Annual Day function
Part (b): 2.25 times
Part (c): names the natural world / surroundings as affected, with the link to society
Part (d): chooses a proposal and justifies with the data and the chapter

questions.q: The page numbers of this book follow a butterfly and a paper plane. (a) What lesson does the chapter draw from them? (b) What did a simple paper plane lead to, as the chapter tells it?
questions.a: (a) Learning takes flight when curiosity leads the way. (b) A paper plane inspired real scientific explorations of flight, from early inventors studying bird wings to engineers designing aircraft.

Part (b): explorations of flight / bird wings to aircraft

questions.a: (a) Also about responsibility. (b) Human activities are linked to what happens in the natural world and to the society we live in. (c) Science can help address environmental challenges and help create a more sustainable world. (d) Aisha is not right; science brings both discovery and responsibility.

Part (b): link to the natural world and society
Part (c): environmental challenges / sustainable world
Part (d): verdict that Aisha is wrong with the reason

questions.q: The chapter says science can help in 'creating a more sustainable world'. (a) What does it say science can help to address? (b) Give one example of your own where a student's science could do this in a school.
questions.a: (a) Environmental challenges. (b) For example, finding which events leave the most waste and testing a way to cut it.
s: Part (a): environmental challenges
Part (b): a sensible school example

questions.q: Compare the questions 'What is this called?' and 'Why does this happen the way it does?' Which is closer to the Grade 7 aim in the chapter? Use a lamp or a paper plane to give both questions an example.
questions.a: The second. The chapter says Grade 7 asks deeper questions: how things work, why events happen, what patterns mean. Example: 'What is a paper plane called?' versus 'Why does a paper plane with a sharp nose go farther?'

Gives the chapter's reason: Grade 7 asks deeper questions
Gives a matching pair of questions on one object

questions.q: (a) Name the three items the chapter says we play with to look for other properties of materials. (b) Which question about them leads to classifying materials, and into which two groups?
questions.a: (a) Electric batteries, lamps and wires. (b) 'What kind of materials do we need to make a lamp glow?' It leads to metals and non-metals.

Part (b): the lamp-glow question and the groups metals and non-metals

questions.q: Which pair of everyday puzzles does the chapter use to begin its tour of the properties of materials?
questions.a: Why some fruits are sour, and what a haldi stain does when washed
o: Why some fruits are sour, and what a haldi stain does when washed
Why a lamp glows, and what happens when a battery runs out
Why ice melts, and where rain goes when it trickles down
Why fruits ripen, and why rocks break into pebbles

questions.q:
The canteen of a school in Kolhapur plans to keep ice for sherbet during the 100-minute sports-day programme. A trial with a block of ice in each of three containers, kept in the same warm room, gave the following times before it melted completely: open steel glass, 15 minutes; closed steel box, 45 minutes; thermos flask, 150 minutes. A glass costs ₹30, a box ₹120 and a flask ₹400. Ice can be refilled at no cost.
(a) The chapter links the melting of ice to a topic of its tour. Name it and say what the ice is receiving.
(b) How many times longer did the ice last in the flask than in the open glass?
(c) Which containers alone can hold ice for the whole 100 minutes without a refill?
(d) The canteen can spend up to ₹400. Choose a plan and justify it with your answers.
questions.a: (a) How heat flows; the ice receives heat from the surroundings. (b) 150/15 = 10 times. (c) Only the flask (150 min); the box lasts 45 min, so it needs refills at about 45 and 90 min. (d) Either with reasons: one flask at ₹400 (no refill, but uses the whole budget), or three boxes at ₹360 refilled twice (cheaper but needs staff time).
s: Part (a): heat flow, ice receives heat
Part (b): 10 times
Part (c): only the flask lasts the whole 100 minutes
Part (d): picks a plan and justifies it using cost and the times

questions.q: Arjun in Chennai watches a kulfi melting in his hand and wonders how the warmth moves from the surroundings into the kulfi. Which topic of the chapter's tour does his question belong to?

questions.q: Dinesh says that the tour could just as well start with the water topic, since 'all of it is science'. Show with one link each why heat must come before water, and changes before heat, in the chapter's tour.
questions.a: Water comes after heat because the Sun's heat evaporates the water from the seas, so we need heat first. Heat comes after changes because some changes happen, or happen faster, when things are heated, and the tour moves on from changes to how heat flows.

(b) The glacier shows the same idea on a very large scale, linking the small ice cube in a glass with a huge natural body of ice.

questions.q: Ananya states, 'A torch battery that has run out can be used again if we wait for a few days.' Show that this statement contradicts the chapter and say what the chapter uses the battery to ask.
questions.a: The chapter says a torch battery runs out eventually and cannot be used again, so waiting does not help. It uses this to ask what kind of changes happen around us, since some changes can be reversed and others cannot.

Shows the contradiction with waiting

questions.q:
A village near Dehradun records its well's water level as the distance of the water below ground: April, 9 m; July, 8 m; September, 5 m; December, 6 m. The panchayat is deciding whether to limit the use of pumps from March to May. Farmer Ramesh says there is plenty of water because the level in September is high. The Sarpanch points out that the level in April was lower.
(a) In which month is the water closest to the ground, and which step in the chapter's route of water happened just before?
(b) By how many metres did the water rise between April and September?
(c) Between September and the next April the level would fall by how many metres if it returned to 9 m, and what does that suggest about the pumps?
(d) Decide whether the panchayat should limit pumping from March to May and justify with the data and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) September, with the rain having trickled underground. (b) 9 - 5 = 4 m. (c) 9 - 5 = 4 m again; the level falls over the dry months, so using the pumps heavily then could leave the well too low. (d) Yes, limiting is supported: the water in the well comes from rain trickling down, which arrives in the monsoon, and the April level is lowest; arguments for not limiting must also use the data.
s: Part (a): September; rain falling and trickling underground
Part (b): 4 m
Part (c): 4 m fall, suggesting a lower level in dry months
Part (d): decision with reasoning from the data and the route of water

questions.q: Why does the chapter begin with things 'we experience but perhaps never ask questions about'? State the aim of this opening in two points.
questions.a: It shows that ordinary materials around us, such as sour fruits and haldi stains, hold science, and it invites us to start by asking questions about them.
s: Says ordinary materials hold science questions
Says the aim is to start by asking questions

questions.q: Hema writes that ice melting, a battery running out and fruits ripening are all changes, so all three can be reversed easily. Find the flaw using the chapter and state which of her examples the chapter itself says cannot be reversed.
questions.a: The flaw is that the chapter says some changes can be reversed and others cannot, so being a change does not mean it can be reversed. The torch battery that has run out cannot be used again.

questions.q: Describe in words a set-up to sort five objects of your choice into those that make a lamp glow and those that do not. Say (a) what you connect, (b) how you test each object, (c) what you record, (d) what group names the chapter points to, and (e) one new question the result raises.

Part (b): tests the objects one at a time
Part (c): records glows or not
Part (d): metals and non-metals
Part (e): a sensible new question

questions.q:
On Sports Day at a school in Ranchi the wall clock stops. The teacher plants a pole in the ground and Aman marks the tip of its shadow with a pebble each hour on a sunny morning. The distances of the tip from the pole's base were: 8 a.m., 140 cm; 9 a.m., 95 cm; 10 a.m., 60 cm; 11 a.m., 40 cm. Clouds cover the Sun from 11.30 a.m. to 1.30 p.m. The events are: march-past at 8.30, relay at 11, lunch announcement at 12.30 and prize distribution under floodlights at 6.30 p.m.
(a) For what purpose does the chapter say early humans used the position of shadows?
(b) By how many centimetres did the shadow shorten from 8 a.m. to 11 a.m.?
(c) A pebble now lies 75 cm from the base. Between which two hours was it placed?
(d) Which of the four events can the pole time and which need a watch? Justify.
questions.a: (a) To tell the time. (b) 140 - 40 = 100 cm. (c) Between 9 a.m. (95 cm) and 10 a.m. (60 cm). (d) The pole can time the 8.30 march-past and the 11 a.m. relay, which fall in sunshine. The 12.30 announcement is under cloud (no Sun-shadow), and the 6.30 p.m. function is after sunset; both need a watch.
s: Part (a): telling the time
Part (b): 100 cm
Part (c): between 9 a.m. and 10 a.m.
Part (d): sorts the events, using Sun-shadow availability

questions.q: Compare how people told the time before the age of electric clocks and digital watches with how we tell it today. Name one method of each.
questions.a: Before: they used the position of shadows of objects in the Sun. Today: electric clocks and digital wrist watches.
s: Names the shadow method
Names electric or digital clocks/watches today

questions.q: Arvind says, 'We have lamps for the night and clocks for the time, so there is no need to study light and shadows now.' Argue for and against, then give a verdict. Use the chapter.
questions.a: For: we can generate light to read at night and watches tell the time. Against: questions about the nature of light gave a deep understanding of the universe, and shadows of the Earth and Moon lead to eclipses. Verdict: study is still needed because the chapter says light and shadows reach beyond the things at home.
s: Gives a point for Arvind's view from the chapter
Gives a point against: deep understanding of the universe
Gives a second point against: Earth and Moon shadows and eclipses
Gives a verdict
Justifies the verdict with the chapter

questions.q: The chapter says the Earth rotates on its axis, the Moon goes around the Earth and the Earth goes around the Sun. (a) Which of these movements involves the Moon? (b) Which two bodies cast the shadows that lead to eclipses?
questions.a: (a) The Moon going around the Earth. (b) The Earth and the Moon.
s: Part (a): the Moon going around the Earth
Part (b): the Earth and the Moon

questions.q: The chapter asks, 'But why animals alone?' after naming what animals need. In five marks: (a) list three things the chapter says animals need or do to survive and grow, (b) write the question it asks about plants for each, where it asks one, and (c) say what this way of asking shows about how science works.
questions.a: (a) Eat, breathe, and have blood circulate the nutrients around the body. (b) For eating: how do plants get their food? For breathing: do they also breathe, and how? (c) Science extends a question from one case to another to look for what living things share.
s: Part (a): three things animals do or need
Part (b): the plant questions matching food and breathing
Part (c): science extends questions to other cases

questions.q:
Class 7B is printing 300 notices for a sky-watching evening at a school in Pune. The notice says: 'To follow eclipses and day and night, learn that the Earth rotates on its axis and that the Moon goes around the Earth.' The teacher says one movement is missing. The notices are already printed at ₹2 each. Reprinting all 300 would cost ₹2 each again. A rubber stamp adding the missing line to every notice costs ₹150.
(a) Which movement is missing from the notice?
(b) Which two bodies cast the shadows that lead to eclipses?
(c) How much more does reprinting cost than the stamp?
(d) Choose reprint or stamp and justify, using your answers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Earth going around the Sun. (b) The Earth and the Moon. (c) Reprint = 300 x 2 = ₹600; 600 - 150 = ₹450 more. (d) Either with reasons: the stamp, since the chapter lists three movements and the stamp adds the third at a quarter of the cost; reprint only if the stamped notice looks too untidy.
s: Part (a): the Earth going around the Sun
Part (b): the Earth and the Moon
Part (c): ₹450 more
Part (d): picks one and justifies with cost and the chapter's three movements

questions.q: Reverse: the result reads 'a person can tell the time without any clock.' Describe a situation, using the chapter, that produces this result, and list what is needed for it to work.
questions.a: A person fixes a stick or pole in sunlit ground and reads the time from where its shadow falls, as early humans did. Needed: the Sun to be shining, an object to cast a shadow, and a way to note the position of the shadow.
s: Describes the shadow-position method
Names the Sun as necessary
Names an object and recording the position

questions.q: The chapter says light helps us see. What does it say is more important about asking questions on the nature of light? Add one thing the chapter says about how we make light today.
questions.a: Asking questions about the nature of light has given a very deep understanding of the universe. Today we have developed many ways to generate light, so we can read a book at night when the Sun does not shine.
s: States the deep understanding of the universe
States that we generate light to read at night
